column59: Day 1 food needs to improve. Boxed lunches are efficient but not ideal to an audience who pays a lot of money to attend. Day 2 breakfast and lunch was better and what people probably expect at a conference. Also I know Andreas said scheduling fell through at the Peter O' Donell building but FIPS 'n' Chips 2027 has to all be in one place with multiple rooms like ICMC if it wants to compete even if that means UT students can't come. Perhaps a pre-conference day for the UT students can take place on a Monday as I'm sure most people don't like traveling on a weekend anyways. Conference should also maybe take place first week of November or start later in the week next year to avoid ACL and F1 weekend congestion issues.

column96: "PANEL — Where Randomness Begins: Physical or Not?" Thought provoking and audience engagement was good to hear.
column110: "PANEL — ISO/IEC 19790:2025 Adoption". Was good to hear CMVP's perspective on how this standard would evolve to FIPS 140-4. However with a hot topic that would inevitably have a lot of comments or questions, the track should have allotted at least 15 minutes dedicated to questions.
column125: All were good. I think panels should have allotted time for questions for the audience rather than rushing for only 1-2 questions if the panel talks to long on their own. Also please don't make the most important presentation the very first one of the day. If you're late due to unpredictable Austin traffic your SOL.
column126: "When AI Meets Cybersecurity" & "ISO/IEC 19790:2025 Adoption" as these will both be relevant for sure. I'd like to see AI and how it's integrated into vendor/lab work flows. Concerns and pitfalls of using AI in the validation process would be good to hear.
column127: A couple live demos would be nice to see and more audience engagement in some talks would be nice. Even some questions from the speaker to the audience would be good.
column129: The event in Austin or at least in the surrounding area (round rock, cedar park etc ) :).
column130: Things that only atsec/CVA can control. Food and time between and after tracks. Take a look at the recent OpenSSL Conference and old RSA conferences were handled. People of course learned a lot and networked but they also walked away thinking they had a lot of fun. That should be the goal so people look forward to coming back in subsequent years. Make little side games between tracks or during breaks (prizes, challenges or things to do in the lobby would be fun). Entertainment might not be a bad idea to wake people up after lunch. Also most of these people aren't going to explore Austin on their own so setting up a small event or get together after dinner is more fun than going back to a hotel room. Could just inform everyone that the dinners are pay yourself but a reservation a local restaurant would be nice.
column139: Nope, thanks for putting it all on! I know it's a tremendous amount of work and the community appreciates it!

I attended the beginner track to be able to present to my team the FIPS process and build their understanding. I have a decent level of knowledge of what goes into FIPS, but I have never been a tester (I am a customer facing field engineer) and this track helped me solidify my training plan for my team. column32:
I liked how the talk explained the importance of designing quantum-safe and cryptographically agile Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) to protect sensitive information against evolving cybersecurity threats. I found it interesting to learn how organizations can prepare for future risks from quantum computing by adopting post-quantum cryptography and building flexible security systems.

My personal takeaway was that cybersecurity professionals need to think ahead and develop solutions that can adapt to emerging threats. This talk connects to my career goals in cybersecurity and cloud computing because I want to develop the skills needed to protect sensitive data, strengthen security infrastructure, and help organizations stay prepared for new technologies. Learning about quantum-safe security also motivated me to continue exploring advanced cryptography and how it can be applied to real-world security challenges.
column34: The panel provided valuable insights into the growing intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity, particularly the challenges facing current cryptographic testing and validation processes. I appreciated the discussion on the need for scalable, adaptable, and forward-looking security approaches to address emerging threats. Additional real-world case studies and practical examples of how AI can strengthen cryptographic testing, improve threat detection, and support compliance would further enhance the learning experience. Overall, the session was informative and relevant to my professional development and long-term career goals in cybersecurity and cloud computing.

column32:
I've seen some concerning patterns within our own organization of relying too heavily on LLM's without the skills, knowledge, capabilities or know-how to call them out when they hallucinate. The speaker said something to the affect of "Study finds that developers using LLM's to implement security code without fully understanding the standards themselves to properly guide the LLM model have a tendency to write far more insecure code. Without full understanding or ability to call out the LLM on mistakes, a false sense of confidence is established that the code is 'highly secure' when it is actually very insecure". That's a lesson we all need to be aware of in the day of AI assisted development.

The second talk on 140-4 was a little concerning, for example we received an RFQ as recently as September 16th 2026 asking for a FIPS 140-2 module. The industry is still being educated that 140-2 is end of life, have not completed the transition to 140-3 and we're already talking about 140-4. It feels like this could further erode trust in the FIPS program because we all know once 140-4 is out and the 3 and 4 letter agencies learn about it, they will always require the latest and greatest so 140-3 would be dead before it even got off the ground.

column32: Day 1 had a lot of great sessions from the keynote by Kevin to the hilarious theater show at the end. Kevin’s presentation (and the panels with Tim, Kailai, etc) was valuable as it gave me a view of CMVP, who is who, and where they are going. Jeff’s talk on machine authentication directly addresses a problem I’m facing in silicon chip design as we move to chiplet and more complex SoC architectures where we have a diverse set of processors and accelerators with various levels of trust and cryptographic relevance crammed into a single package that has to be “FIPS certifiable”. The entropy panel opened my eyes to some of the holes in our own design and understanding of entropy sources - we just pick a noise source IP and rely on the vendors claims - and how much better we can be at that. The second day brought a lot of the ISO work Eric talks about in our SNIA security WG into focus and let me see the direct ramifications of something as seemingly minor as reordering a list of requirements.

For the AI meets Cybersecurity panel, having panelists from both AI and Cybersecurity backgrounds made the discussion richer, providing different perspectives on topics like the asymmetry between an attacker and defender. This panel also introduced me to a new concept of grounding agentic trust in cryptography, so that even when an agent may behave unpredictably, the system can still approve its actions before it takes them. 
For Trust without Boundaries, this was my first introduction to composable assurance and the challenges single-chip and SoC manufacturers face with validation. Learning that the traditional cryptographic boundary model no longer fits how products are built today gave me a better sense of where validation is heading and how much validation has to evolve alongside technology.
